group: Era 3: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era
title: Era 3 Quizzes (The Renaissance & Early Modern Era) — Batch 2 of 2
subtitle: Questions 1–141 · Authenticated UGC NET Stems, Keys & Explanations

items.title: Quiz Q#251 · Thomas Nashe
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas Nashe
items.stem: In which court interlude by Thomas Nashe does King Henry VIII's former jester Will Summers act as a satirical presenter and commentator while the dying king Summer reviews his attendants?
items.explanation: Will Summers is the chorus and comic commentator in Thomas Nashe's Summer's Last Will and Testament (1592/1600), mocking the formal seasonal pageantry.

items.title: Quiz Q#252 · Thomas Nashe
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas Nashe
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Brightness falls from the air."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Thomas Nashe's Summer’s Last Will and Testament (1600).

items.title: Quiz Q#253 · Thomas Nashe
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas Nashe
items.stem: Which 1592 dramatic interlude by Thomas Nashe was performed at Archbishop John Whitgift's palace at Croydon during an outbreak of the London plague, featuring the haunting lyric 'Brightness falls from the air'?
items.explanation: Summer's Last Will and Testament (1600) was staged at Croydon Palace in autumn 1592 while London theatres were closed by plague, containing Nashe's famous plague dirge.

items.title: Quiz Q#254 · Thomas Nashe
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas Nashe
items.stem: In which 1594 picaresque prose narrative by Thomas Nashe does the rogue page Jack Wilton journey through Renaissance Europe, witnessing the Battle of Marignano, Erasmus, and the execution of Cutwolfe in Rome?
items.explanation: Jack Wilton is the rogue hero and first-person narrator of Thomas Nashe's The Unfortunate Traveller: or, the Life of Jack Wilton (1594).

items.title: Quiz Q#255 · Thomas Nashe
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas Nashe
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Revenge is the glory of arms."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Thomas Nashe's The Unfortunate Traveller (1594).

items.title: Quiz Q#256 · Thomas Nashe
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas Nashe
items.stem: Which groundbreaking 1594 prose narrative by Thomas Nashe is widely celebrated as the earliest picaresque novel in English literature, combining rogue autobiography, historical fiction, and grotesque violence?
items.explanation: The Unfortunate Traveller (1594) established the English picaresque tradition, blending episodic travel narrative, historical parody, and vivid colloquial prose.

items.title: Quiz Q#257 · Ben Jonson
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Ben Jonson
items.stem: In which comedy of humours by Ben Jonson does the anxious father Knowell spy on his son Edward in London, accompanied by the braggart soldier Captain Bobadill?
items.explanation: Knowell and Captain Bobadill are central figures in Ben Jonson's Every Man in His Humour (1598/1601), the landmark comedy that launched Jonson's theory of humours.

items.title: Quiz Q#258 · Ben Jonson
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Ben Jonson
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"And sport with human follies, not with crimes."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Ben Jonson's Every Man in His Humour (1601, revised in the 1616 folio).

items.title: Quiz Q#259 · Ben Jonson
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Ben Jonson
items.stem: Which 1598 satirical comedy by Ben Jonson, famously performed by the Lord Chamberlain's Men with William Shakespeare in the cast, established the dramatic genre of the 'Comedy of Humours'?
items.explanation: Every Man in His Humour (1598) established the comedy of humours on the English stage; Shakespeare performed in the original production at the Curtain Theatre.

items.title: Quiz Q#260 · Ben Jonson
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Ben Jonson
items.stem: Which 1616 collection of short poems by Ben Jonson, described by the poet as 'the ripest of my studies', contains his moving elegies 'On My First Daughter' and 'On My First Son'?
items.explanation: Epigrams (1616) contains Ben Jonson's classical epigrams, including the immortal elegy 'On My First Son' ('Farewell, thou child of my right hand').

items.title: Quiz Q#261 · Ben Jonson
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Ben Jonson
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Farewell, thou child of my right hand."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Ben Jonson's Epigrams (1616).

items.title: Quiz Q#262 · Ben Jonson
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Ben Jonson
items.stem: Which collection of 133 short classical poems published in Ben Jonson's 1616 Works includes his verse epistles to King James, sharp satirical portraits, and the famous praise of William Camden?
items.explanation: Jonson's Epigrams (1616) represented his conscious emulation of the Roman poet Martial, combining moral satire with poignant personal epitaphs.

items.title: Quiz Q#263 · Ben Jonson
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Ben Jonson
items.stem: In Ben Jonson's city comedy The Alchemist, which cunning butler assumes the pseudonym 'Captain Face' to operate a fraudulent alchemy scam in his master Lovewit's Blackfriars house?
items.explanation: Jeremy the butler disguises himself as Captain Face in The Alchemist (1610/12), forming an unholy triumvirate of cheats with Subtle and Dol Common.

items.title: Quiz Q#264 · Ben Jonson
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Ben Jonson
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"I will have all my beds blown up."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Ben Jonson's The Alchemist (1612).

items.title: Quiz Q#265 · Ben Jonson
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Ben Jonson
items.stem: Which satirical comedy by Ben Jonson adheres strictly to the classical unities of time, place, and action, depicting a single afternoon of swindling Sir Epicure Mammon, Tribulation Wholesome, and Kastril in London?
items.explanation: The Alchemist (1612) is renowned for its technical perfection in observing the classical unities while delivering a relentless satire of human greed and gullibility.

items.title: Quiz Q#266 · Ben Jonson
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Ben Jonson
items.stem: Which 1616 poetry collection by Ben Jonson includes 'To Penshurst', celebrated as the pioneering country-house poem in English literature, and the famous song 'To Celia'?
items.explanation: The Forest (published in Jonson's 1616 Workes) contains 15 major poems including 'To Penshurst' (praising the Sidney estate) and 'Song: To Celia' ('Drink to me only with thine eyes').

items.title: Quiz Q#267 · Ben Jonson
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Ben Jonson
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Come, my Celia, let us prove."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Ben Jonson's The Forest (1616).

items.title: Quiz Q#268 · Ben Jonson
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Ben Jonson
items.stem: Which lyrical collection by Ben Jonson contains his celebrated verse epistle 'To Penshurst', establishing the English genre of country-house poetry celebrating hospitable estates and social harmony?
items.explanation: The Forest (1616) contains 'To Penshurst', which inaugurated the English country-house poem tradition later followed by Carew, Herrick, and Marvell.

items.title: Quiz Q#269 · Ben Jonson
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Ben Jonson
items.stem: Which posthumous 1641 collection of critical reflections, commonplace notes, and aphorisms by Ben Jonson contains his famous evaluation of Shakespeare ('I loved the man, and do honour his memory, on this side idolatry, as much as any')?
items.explanation: Timber, or Discoveries (1641) is Jonson's critical notebook, containing his judicious assessment of Shakespeare, Francis Bacon, and the art of English prose style.

items.title: Quiz Q#270 · Ben Jonson
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Ben Jonson
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Language most shows a man."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Ben Jonson's Timber, or Discoveries (1641).

items.title: Quiz Q#271 · Ben Jonson
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Ben Jonson
items.stem: Which critical volume by Ben Jonson, subtitled 'Explorata' or 'Discoveries made upon men and matter', represents one of the earliest sustained works of literary criticism and prose aphorisms in English?
items.explanation: Timber, or Discoveries (1641) contains Jonson's observations on rhetoric, poetry, and philosophy, drawing upon Seneca, Quintilian, and Erasmus.

items.title: Quiz Q#272 · Ben Jonson
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Ben Jonson
items.stem: Which posthumous poetry collection of Ben Jonson (published in the 1640 Second Folio) contains his celebrated tribute 'To the Memory of My Beloved the Author, Mr. William Shakespeare', hailing him as 'not of an age, but for all time'?
items.explanation: Underwood (1640) collects Jonson's later lyric poetry, including his famous eulogy on William Shakespeare and 'A Fit of Rhyme against Rhyme'.

items.title: Quiz Q#273 · Ben Jonson
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Ben Jonson
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"It is not growing like a tree."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Ben Jonson's Underwood (1640).

items.title: Quiz Q#274 · Ben Jonson
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Ben Jonson
items.stem: Which posthumous collection of Ben Jonson's later verse, named to signify a lesser grove of trees compared to his earlier volume The Forest, contains 'An Ode to Himself' and his 'Celebration of Charis'?
items.explanation: Underwood (1640) was organized by Jonson as a companion sequel to The Forest, preserving his mature Cavalier lyrics and critical odes.

items.title: Quiz Q#275 · Ben Jonson
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Ben Jonson
items.stem: In which satirical masterpiece by Ben Jonson does a childless Venetian magnifico feign mortal illness to dupe the legacy-hunters Voltore (the vulture), Corbaccio (the raven), and Corvino (the crow)?
items.explanation: Volpone (1607) features the titular fox Volpone and his parasite Mosca orchestrating elaborate swindles against greedy Venetian legacy hunters.

items.title: Quiz Q#276 · Ben Jonson
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Ben Jonson
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Good morning to the day."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Ben Jonson's Volpone (1607).

items.title: Quiz Q#277 · Ben Jonson
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Ben Jonson
items.stem: Which beast-fable satire by Ben Jonson, set in decadent Renaissance Venice, opens with the blasphemous morning invocation: 'Good morning to the day; and next, my gold! / Open the shrine, that I may see my saint'?
items.explanation: Volpone; or, The Fox (1607) opens with Volpone worshiping his gold as his god, establishing Jonson's scathing satire of Renaissance avarice.

items.title: Quiz Q#278 · Ben Jonson
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Ben Jonson
items.stem: In Ben Jonson's city comedy Bartholomew Fair, which overzealous magistrate disguises himself in fool's clothing as 'Mad Arthur' to uncover the 'enormities' of the Smithfield fairgrounds?
items.explanation: Justice Adam Overdo is the comic magistrate in Bartholomew Fair (1614) whose efforts to expose fairground vice repeatedly land him in the stocks.

items.title: Quiz Q#279 · Ben Jonson
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Ben Jonson
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Which is your best actor now?"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Ben Jonson's Bartholomew Fair (1631).

items.title: Quiz Q#280 · Ben Jonson
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Ben Jonson
items.stem: Which panoramic Jacobean comedy by Ben Jonson brings together a vast spectrum of London street life—including the puritan hypocrite Zeal-of-the-Land Busy, the pig-woman Ursula, and a profane puppet show—at Smithfield?
items.explanation: Bartholomew Fair (1614) is Jonson's most vibrant London comedy, satirizing religious hypocrisy, bureaucratic vanity, and fairground trickery.

items.title: Quiz Q#281 · John Donne
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Donne
items.stem: Which 1624 prose masterpiece by John Donne, composed during a dangerous bout of typhus fever, contains Meditation XVII featuring the phrases 'No man is an island' and 'for whom the bell tolls'?
items.explanation: Devotions upon Emergent Occasions (1624) records Donne's spiritual and psychological reflections as he lay dangerously ill at St. Paul's Deanery.

items.title: Quiz Q#282 · John Donne
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Donne
items.stem: Which devotional prose work by John Donne is formally organized into 23 chapters corresponding to the 23 stages of his physical illness, each comprising a Meditation, an Expostulation, and a Prayer?
items.explanation: Devotions upon Emergent Occasions (1624) uses a strict tripartite structure (Meditation, Expostulation with God, Prayer) for each stage of his sickness and recovery.

items.title: Quiz Q#283 · John Donne
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Donne
items.stem: Which sequence of 19 Metaphysical devotional poems by John Donne contains passionate theological pleas including 'Batter my heart, three-person'd God' and 'Death, be not proud'?
items.explanation: John Donne's Holy Sonnets (written c. 1609-10, published 1633) blend Petrarchan sonnet structure with intense spiritual anxiety over salvation, judgment, and divine grace.

items.title: Quiz Q#284 · John Donne
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Donne
items.stem: In which sequence of devotional lyrics does John Donne dramatize the sinner's terror of damnation, begging God to 'break, blow, burn, and make me new' in Sonnet XIV?
items.explanation: Holy Sonnets (1633) features Donne's striking metaphysical conceits applied to sacred theology, notably in the violent assault imagery of 'Batter my heart'.

items.title: Quiz Q#285 · John Donne
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Donne
items.stem: Which posthumously published 1633 collection of secular love poetry by John Donne revolutionized English verse through startling metaphysical conceits in poems like 'The Flea', 'The Sun Rising', and 'The Canonization'?
items.explanation: Songs and Sonnets (1633) established John Donne's reputation for dramatic colloquial openings, intellectual wit, and unconventional love conceits.

items.title: Quiz Q#286 · John Donne
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Donne
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Busy old fool, unruly sun."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in John Donne's Songs and Sonnets (1633).

items.title: Quiz Q#287 · John Donne
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Donne
items.stem: Which landmark collection of Metaphysical love lyrics features the famous conceit comparing parted lovers to the stiff twin legs of a draftsman's compass in 'A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning'?
items.explanation: Donne's Songs and Sonnets contains 'A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning', whose compass conceit was famously analyzed by Dr. Samuel Johnson in his Life of Cowley.

items.title: Quiz Q#288 · Thomas Dekker
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas Dekker
items.stem: In which 1600 romantic folk play by Thomas Dekker does the goddess Fortune offer an impoverished Cypriot beggar the choice of wisdom, strength, health, beauty, long life, or an inexhaustible purse of gold?
items.explanation: Old Fortunatus (1600) by Thomas Dekker is a morality-infused romantic comedy dramatizing the tragic curse of choosing worldly riches over wisdom.

items.title: Quiz Q#289 · Thomas Dekker
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas Dekker
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"There's a lean fellow beats all conquerors."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Thomas Dekker's Old Fortunatus (1600).

items.title: Quiz Q#290 · Thomas Dekker
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas Dekker
items.stem: Which poetic fantasy drama by Thomas Dekker, performed before Queen Elizabeth at Christmas 1599, blends German folklore with English stage romance to depict the tragic hubris of Fortunatus and his sons?
items.explanation: Old Fortunatus (1600) combines Dekker's lyrical blank verse with allegorical pageantry featuring Fortune, Virtue, and Vice.

items.title: Quiz Q#291 · Thomas Dekker
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas Dekker
items.stem: In Thomas Dekker's The Shoemaker's Holiday, which hearty, eccentric master craftsman rises to become Lord Mayor of London and hosts a pancake feast for all London apprentices on Shrove Tuesday?
items.explanation: Simon Eyre is the jovial, swearing master shoemaker whose rapid social elevation drives the festive plot of Thomas Dekker's The Shoemaker's Holiday (1599/1600).

items.title: Quiz Q#292 · Thomas Dekker
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas Dekker
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Cold's the wind, and wet's the rain."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Thomas Dekker's The Shoemaker’s Holiday (1600).

items.title: Quiz Q#293 · Thomas Dekker
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas Dekker
items.stem: Which 1599 citizen comedy by Thomas Dekker celebrates London's craft guilds and depicts the romantic sub-plot of nobleman Rowland Lacy disguising himself as the Dutch shoemaker Hans Meulter?
items.explanation: The Shoemaker's Holiday (1600) is Dekker's joyful celebration of Elizabethan merchant and artisan culture, drawn from Thomas Deloney's The Gentle Craft.

items.title: Quiz Q#294 · John Marston
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Marston
items.stem: In which 1605 Jacobean city comedy by John Marston does young Freevill renounce the vindictive Dutch courtesan Franceschina to wed the virtuous Beatrice, while testing his puritanical friend Malheureux?
items.explanation: The Dutch Courtezan (1605) by John Marston contrasts romantic constancy and sexual obsession with the comic sub-plot of the trickster Cocledemoy.

items.title: Quiz Q#295 · John Marston
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Marston
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"The dark is my delight."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in John Marston's The Dutch Courtezan (1605).

items.title: Quiz Q#296 · John Marston
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Marston
items.stem: Which satirical comedy by John Marston features the knavish rogue Cocledemoy repeatedly swindling the pious, money-grubbing tavern keeper Mulligrub in a series of farcical London practical jokes?
items.explanation: The Dutch Courtezan (1605) balances dark moral debate with the broad citizen farce of Cocledemoy's comic trickery against Mulligrub.

items.title: Quiz Q#297 · John Marston
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Marston
items.stem: In John Marston's dark satirical drama The Malcontent, which deposed Duke of Genoa disguises himself as the railing, cynical courtier Malevole to expose court degeneracy and regain his throne?
items.explanation: Malevole is the bitter, satirical disguise of Duke Altofronto in Marston's The Malcontent (1604), embodying the Jacobean stock type of the satirical malcontent.

items.title: Quiz Q#298 · John Marston
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Marston
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Discord to malcontents is very manna."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in John Marston's The Malcontent (1604).

items.title: Quiz Q#299 · John Marston
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Marston
items.stem: Which 1604 tragicomedy by John Marston was performed by the Children of the Queen's Revels at Blackfriars, later published with a celebrated Induction written by John Webster featuring the actors Burbage and Condell?
items.explanation: The Malcontent (1604) is Marston's masterwork, blending Senecan revenge motifs with biting satirical comedy in an Italianate court setting.

items.title: Quiz Q#300 · Francis Beaumont (1584–1616) and John Fletcher
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Francis Beaumont (1584–1616) and John Fletcher
items.stem: In Beaumont and Fletcher's romantic tragicomedy Philaster, which rightful heir to the Sicilian throne falls in love with Princess Arethusa and accepts the service of the devoted page Bellario (Euphrasia in disguise)?
options: The Knight of the Burning Pestle
items.explanation: Philaster; or, Love Lies a-Bleeding (c. 1609/1620) established Beaumont and Fletcher's signature genre of courtly tragicomedy with intricate emotional dilemmas.

items.title: Quiz Q#301 · Francis Beaumont (1584–1616) and John Fletcher
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Francis Beaumont (1584–1616) and John Fletcher
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"The devil take the hindmost."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Francis Beaumont (1584–1616) and John Fletcher's Philaster (1620).

items.title: Quiz Q#302 · Francis Beaumont (1584–1616) and John Fletcher
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Francis Beaumont (1584–1616) and John Fletcher
items.stem: Which celebrated tragicomedy by Francis Beaumont and John Fletcher, subtitled 'Love Lies a-Bleeding', popularized the Jacobean taste for melodramatic reversals, courtly sentiment, and female page disguises?
options: The Knight of the Burning Pestle
items.explanation: Philaster (c. 1609) was the King's Men's major stage hit, initiating the collaborative tragicomedies that dominated Jacobean and Caroline theatrical fashion.

items.title: Quiz Q#303 · Francis Beaumont (1584–1616) and John Fletcher
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Francis Beaumont (1584–1616) and John Fletcher
items.stem: In Beaumont and Fletcher's metatheatrical satire The Knight of the Burning Pestle, which grocer's apprentice is thrust onto the stage by a vocal London Citizen and his Wife to perform chivalric heroics?
options: The Knight of the Burning Pestle
items.explanation: Rafe the apprentice is instructed by George and Nell to play the heroic Knight of the Burning Pestle in Beaumont's 1607 theatrical parody.

items.title: Quiz Q#304 · Francis Beaumont (1584–1616) and John Fletcher
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Francis Beaumont (1584–1616) and John Fletcher
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Nose, nose, jolly red nose."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Francis Beaumont (1584–1616) and John Fletcher's The Knight of the Burning Pestle (1613).

items.title: Quiz Q#305 · Francis Beaumont (1584–1616) and John Fletcher
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Francis Beaumont (1584–1616) and John Fletcher
items.stem: Which brilliant 1607 satirical play by Francis Beaumont is celebrated as the first sustained parody of chivalric romances on the English stage, featuring audience intervention that disrupts the play-within-a-play?
options: The Knight of the Burning Pestle
items.explanation: The Knight of the Burning Pestle (1607/1613) parodied citizen tastes and chivalric tales, closely mirroring the satire of Cervantes' Don Quixote.

items.title: Quiz Q#306 · Francis Beaumont (1584–1616) and John Fletcher
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Francis Beaumont (1584–1616) and John Fletcher
items.stem: In Beaumont and Fletcher's tragedy The Maid's Tragedy, which young nobleman is forced by the King to marry Evadne, only to be told by her on their wedding night that she is the King's secret mistress?
options: The Knight of the Burning Pestle
items.explanation: Amintor is the conflicted protagonist of The Maid's Tragedy (c. 1610/1619), caught between loyalty to his sovereign and agonizing personal dishonour.

items.title: Quiz Q#307 · Francis Beaumont (1584–1616) and John Fletcher
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Francis Beaumont (1584–1616) and John Fletcher
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Die all our faults together."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Francis Beaumont (1584–1616) and John Fletcher's The Maid’s Tragedy (1619).

items.title: Quiz Q#308 · Francis Beaumont (1584–1616) and John Fletcher
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Francis Beaumont (1584–1616) and John Fletcher
items.stem: Which powerful Jacobean tragedy by Beaumont and Fletcher features the tragic death of the rejected maiden Aspatia and the assassination of a lustful tyrant by his defiant mistress Evadne?
options: The Knight of the Burning Pestle
items.explanation: The Maid's Tragedy (1619) is a dark masterpiece of political absolutism, sexual tyranny, and regicide, culminating in widespread catastrophic slaughter.

items.title: Quiz Q#309 · John Webster
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Webster
items.stem: In John Webster's Jacobean masterpiece The Duchess of Malfi, which noble young widow secretly marries her household steward Antonio Bologna, defying the murderous prohibition of her aristocratic brothers?
items.explanation: The Duchess of Malfi is the tragic heroine of Webster's play (1614/1623), celebrated for her dignity when facing torture and strangulation: 'I am Duchess of Malfi still'.

items.title: Quiz Q#310 · John Webster
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Webster
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Cover her face. Mine eyes dazzle."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in John Webster's The Duchess of Malfi (1623).

items.title: Quiz Q#311 · John Webster
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Webster
items.stem: In John Webster's The Duchess of Malfi, which cynical malcontent and palace spy is hired by Duke Ferdinand to oversee the Duchess's torture, only to experience a tragic moral awakening?
items.explanation: Daniel de Bosola is Webster's complex tool-villain who turns against his corrupt employers after witnessing the Duchess's transcendent courage.

items.title: Quiz Q#312 · John Webster
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Webster
items.stem: In John Webster's revenge tragedy The White Devil, which courageous Venetian lady stands trial for adultery and the murder of her husband Camillo, boldly rebuking her accusers in the courtroom scene?
items.explanation: Vittoria Corombona is the defiant protagonist of The White Devil (1612), famously answering Cardinal Monticelso's charges with fierce rhetorical brilliance.

items.title: Quiz Q#313 · John Webster
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Webster
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Call for the robin redbreast and the wren."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in John Webster's The White Devil (1612).

items.title: Quiz Q#314 · John Webster
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Webster
items.stem: Which 1612 revenge tragedy by John Webster, based on the historical Italian murder scandal of Vittoria Accoramboni, features the ruthless Machiavellian tool-villain Flamineo?
items.explanation: The White Devil (1612) established John Webster's dark poetic vision of Italian court corruption, bloody revenge, and moral ambiguity.

items.title: Quiz Q#315 · Thomas Middleton
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas Middleton
items.stem: In Thomas Middleton's London city comedy A Chaste Maid in Cheapside, which virtuous goldsmith's daughter is coerced toward marriage with the dissolute Sir Walter Whorehound while remaining true to Touchwood Junior?
items.explanation: Moll Yellowhammer is the 'chaste maid' in Middleton's bustling city comedy (1613/1630), surrounding her with hypocritical citizens, cuckolded husbands, and fertile gossips.

items.title: Quiz Q#316 · Thomas Middleton
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas Middleton
items.stem: Which biting 1613 London comedy by Thomas Middleton weaves together four intersecting plots of citizen greed, cuckoldry, and arranged marriage, culminating in a farcical christening feast and a staged funeral?
items.explanation: A Chaste Maid in Cheapside (1630) is considered Middleton's masterpiece of Jacobean citizen satire, ruthlessly exposing the commercialization of sex, marriage, and family life.

items.title: Quiz Q#317 · Thomas Middleton
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas Middleton
items.stem: In Middleton and Rowley's tragedy The Changeling, which noblewoman hires the physically repulsive servant De Flores to murder her betrothed Alonzo, only to discover herself bound to De Flores in sexual enslavement?
items.explanation: Beatrice-Joanna hires De Flores to commit murder in The Changeling (1622/1653), leading to the chilling realization that her moral guilt makes them equals: 'Y'are the deed's creature'.

items.title: Quiz Q#318 · Thomas Middleton
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas Middleton
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Y'are the deeds creature."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Thomas Middleton's The Changeling (1653).

items.title: Quiz Q#319 · Thomas Middleton
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas Middleton
items.stem: Which 1622 Jacobean tragedy pairs a dark castle murder plot in Alicante with a comic lunatic-asylum subplot set in the madhouse of Alibius, mirroring themes of moral madness and sexual obsession?
items.explanation: The Changeling (1622) by Thomas Middleton and William Rowley counterpoints Beatrice-Joanna's moral degradation with the madhouse comic antics of Antonio and Franciscus.

items.title: Quiz Q#320 · Thomas Middleton
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas Middleton
items.stem: In Thomas Middleton's Italianate tragedy Women Beware Women, which newlywed Venetian bride is seduced by the Duke of Florence while her naive mother-in-law is distracted by an allegorical game of chess?
items.explanation: Bianca is seduced in Women Beware Women (c. 1621/1657) while Livia plays chess with the mother-in-law, where the moves on the chessboard parallel the seduction above.

items.title: Quiz Q#321 · Thomas Middleton
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas Middleton
items.stem: Which dark Jacobean tragedy by Thomas Middleton culminates in a catastrophic wedding masque where almost the entire court poisons each other through flaming gold arrows, poisoned fumes, and trapdoors?
items.explanation: Women Beware Women features one of the bloodiest climactic masques in Renaissance drama, in which Livia, Guardiano, Hippolito, and Isabella perish in mutual retribution.

items.title: Quiz Q#322 · John Ford
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Ford
items.stem: In John Ford's Spartan tragedy The Broken Heart, which stoic princess continues dancing at a wedding revel upon hearing successive reports of the deaths of her father, friend, and lover, before her heart breaks?
items.explanation: Princess Calantha displays aristocratic Spartan endurance in John Ford's The Broken Heart (1633), calmly crowning her successor before dying of grief.

items.title: Quiz Q#323 · John Ford
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Ford
items.stem: Which Caroline tragedy by John Ford portrays the tragic vengeance of Orgilus against Ithocles and the starvation of Penthea in ancient Sparta, dramatizing aristocratic restraint and quiet despair?
items.explanation: The Broken Heart (1633) is Ford's somber tragedy of repressed passion and stoic honor, noted for its restrained melancholy and formal court rituals.

items.title: Quiz Q#324 · John Ford
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Ford
items.stem: In John Ford's shocking Caroline tragedy 'Tis Pity She's a Whore, which intellectual scholar enters an incestuous romance with his sister Annabella in Parma, entering the final banquet with her heart on his dagger?
items.explanation: Giovanni is the doomed, defiant protagonist of John Ford's 'Tis Pity She's a Whore (1633), whose transgressive love for Annabella ends in carnage and catastrophe.

items.title: Quiz Q#325 · John Ford
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Ford
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"'Tis pity she's a whore."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in John Ford's ’Tis Pity She’s a Whore (1633).

items.title: Quiz Q#326 · John Ford
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Ford
items.stem: Which controversial 1633 tragedy by John Ford explores the tragic fate of siblings Giovanni and Annabella, blending theological sophistry with shocking theatrical violence in decadent Parma?
items.explanation: 'Tis Pity She's a Whore (1633) remains John Ford's most famous and provocative tragedy, examining incest, honor, and vengeance in Caroline theatre.

items.title: Quiz Q#327 · Thomas Hobbes
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas Hobbes
items.stem: In which landmark 1651 political treatise does Thomas Hobbes argue that human life in the state of nature is 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short', necessitating an absolute sovereign commonwealth?
items.explanation: Thomas Hobbes's Leviathan (1651) laid the foundations of modern social contract theory, depicting the sovereign state as an artificial 'mortal god'.

items.title: Quiz Q#328 · Thomas Hobbes
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas Hobbes
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Thomas Hobbes's Leviathan (1651).

items.title: Quiz Q#329 · Thomas Hobbes
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Thomas Hobbes
items.stem: Which 1651 philosophical masterpiece by Thomas Hobbes features an iconic engraved frontispiece showing an immense crowned sovereign composed of hundreds of individual citizens rising above the countryside?
items.explanation: Leviathan (1651) famously visualized the commonwealth as a giant body politic, arguing that rational self-preservation compels subjects to surrender liberties to an absolute sovereign.

items.title: Quiz Q#330 · Robert Herrick
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Robert Herrick
items.stem: Which 1648 collection of over 1,400 lyric poems by Cavalier poet Robert Herrick celebrates English folk customs, maypoles, wassailing, and carpe diem advice in 'To the Virgins, to Make Much of Time'?
items.explanation: Hesperides (1648) collects Robert Herrick's secular Cavalier lyrics celebrating rural festivities, pagan-Christian rituals, and imaginary mistresses.

items.title: Quiz Q#331 · Robert Herrick
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Robert Herrick
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Gather ye rosebuds while ye may."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Robert Herrick's Hesperides (1648).

items.title: Quiz Q#332 · Robert Herrick
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Robert Herrick
items.stem: Which volume of Caroline lyric poetry opens with 'The Argument of His Book' ('I sing of brooks, of blossoms, birds, and bowers / Of April, May, of June, and July flowers')?
items.explanation: Robert Herrick's Hesperides (1648) opens with this famous programmatic poem announcing his celebration of transience, pastoral beauty, and love.

items.title: Quiz Q#333 · Robert Herrick
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Robert Herrick
items.stem: Which collection of religious verse and sacred lyrics was bound and published alongside Robert Herrick's secular volume Hesperides in 1648, featuring 'His Litany to the Holy Spirit'?
items.explanation: His Noble Numbers (1647/48) contains Herrick's devotional poems, offering Christian repentance and pious meditations to balance his secular lyrics.

items.title: Quiz Q#334 · Robert Herrick
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Robert Herrick
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Here a little child I stand."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Robert Herrick's Noble Numbers (1648).

items.title: Quiz Q#335 · Robert Herrick
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Robert Herrick
items.stem: Which devotional work by Robert Herrick, containing poems such as 'A Thanksgiving to God, for His House' and 'To Keep a True Lent', constitutes the pious companion to his Cavalier poems?
items.explanation: Noble Numbers (1648) demonstrated Herrick's devotional voice as an Anglican country parson in Devonshire during the English Civil War.

items.title: Quiz Q#336 · George Herbert
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · George Herbert
items.stem: Which 1633 collection of sacred devotional poems by George Herbert contains concrete pattern poems like 'The Altar' and 'Easter Wings', alongside spiritual dialogues like 'The Collar' and 'Love III'?
items.explanation: The Temple: Sacred Poems and Private Ejaculations (1633) is George Herbert's masterwork of Metaphysical devotional verse, exploring the Christian soul's relationship with God.

items.title: Quiz Q#337 · George Herbert
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · George Herbert
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Love bade me welcome."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in George Herbert's The Temple (1633).

items.title: Quiz Q#338 · George Herbert
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · George Herbert
items.stem: Which volume of Metaphysical devotional verse was delivered on the author's deathbed to his friend Nicholas Ferrar of Little Gidding, with instructions to burn the manuscript if it could not comfort dejected souls?
items.explanation: The Temple (1633) was published posthumously by Nicholas Ferrar, immediately becoming one of the most beloved collections of sacred poetry in English.

items.title: Quiz Q#339 · Izaak Walton
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Izaak Walton
items.stem: In Izaak Walton's The Compleat Angler, which master fisherman acts as teacher and guide, conversing with the hunter Venator and the falconer Auceps on the peaceful virtues of river fishing?
items.explanation: Piscator (the fisherman) is the central narrator and philosophical guide in Izaak Walton's pastoral classic The Compleat Angler (1653).

items.title: Quiz Q#340 · Izaak Walton
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Izaak Walton
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"I am, sir, a Brother of the Angle."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Izaak Walton's The Compleat Angler (1653).

items.title: Quiz Q#341 · Izaak Walton
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Izaak Walton
items.stem: Which celebrated 1653 pastoral prose work by Izaak Walton combines practical instructions on catching trout with pastoral dialogues, fishing songs, and a contemplative retreat from Civil War strife?
items.explanation: The Compleat Angler, or the Contemplative Man's Recreation (1653) celebrated the quiet English countryside, peaceful fellowship, and the spiritual art of angling.

items.title: Quiz Q#342 · Izaak Walton
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Izaak Walton
items.stem: Which classic series of biographical memoirs by Izaak Walton, published between 1640 and 1678, preserved intimate, affectionate portraits of John Donne, George Herbert, and Richard Hooker?
items.explanation: Izaak Walton's Lives established modern English biographical writing, offering vivid firsthand recollections and documentary letters of major Jacobean figures.

items.title: Quiz Q#343 · Izaak Walton
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Izaak Walton
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"For love is a flattering mischief."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Izaak Walton's Lives (1640).

items.title: Quiz Q#344 · Izaak Walton
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Izaak Walton
items.stem: Which pioneering work of English biography began in 1640 as a biographical introduction to John Donne's LXXX Sermons and eventually expanded into a revered gallery of Anglican churchmen and poets?
items.explanation: Walton's Lives originated with his life of John Donne (1640) and grew to include Sir Henry Wotton, Richard Hooker, George Herbert, and Bishop Robert Sanderson.

items.title: Quiz Q#345 · James Shirley
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · James Shirley
items.stem: In James Shirley's 1635 Caroline comedy The Lady of Pleasure, which fashionable wife insists on moving from the country to a lavish London townhouse, indulging in gambling and high-society parties?
items.explanation: Lady Aretina Bornwell is the extravagant social climber whose pursuit of London vanity drives James Shirley's The Lady of Pleasure (1635).

items.title: Quiz Q#346 · James Shirley
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · James Shirley
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Be patient Madam, you may have your pleasure"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in James Shirley's The Lady of Pleasure (1637).

items.title: Quiz Q#347 · James Shirley
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · James Shirley
items.stem: Which 1635 Caroline comedy of manners by James Shirley is celebrated as the direct precursor to Restoration comedies like The Way of the World, satirizing fashionable town gallantry and aristocratic extravagance?
items.explanation: The Lady of Pleasure (1635/37) bridges the Jacobean city comedy and the Restoration comedy of manners through its witty dialogue and satire of London high society.

items.title: Quiz Q#348 · James Shirley
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · James Shirley
items.stem: In James Shirley's 1632 comedy Hyde Park, which independent and teasing heroine subjects her suitors to witty trials during fashionable footraces and horseraces in London's royal park?
items.explanation: Carol is the quick-witted, skeptical heroine of Shirley's Hyde Park (1632), anticipating the independent comedic heroines of the Restoration stage.

items.title: Quiz Q#349 · James Shirley
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · James Shirley
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Never to desire my company"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in James Shirley's Hyde Park (1637).

items.title: Quiz Q#350 · James Shirley
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · James Shirley
items.stem: Which 1632 comedy by James Shirley, licensed just after King Charles I opened Hyde Park to the public, innovated by bringing real contemporary London leisure spots and sporting races directly onto the stage?
items.explanation: Hyde Park (1632/1637) capitalized on the fashionable London craze for the newly opened public park, featuring live sound effects of horse races and footraces.

items.title: Quiz Q#351 · Andrew Marvell
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Andrew Marvell
items.stem: In which 1650 political poem does Andrew Marvell adopt a dignified classical meter to assess Oliver Cromwell's military victories in Ireland while honoring King Charles I's royal composure on the scaffold?
items.explanation: 'An Horatian Ode upon Cromwell's Return from Ireland' (1650/1681) is Marvell's masterpiece of balanced political nuance, evaluating the revolutionary crisis with classical detachment.

items.title: Quiz Q#352 · Andrew Marvell
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Andrew Marvell
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"He nothing common did or mean"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Andrew Marvell's An Horatian Ode (1681).

items.title: Quiz Q#353 · Andrew Marvell
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Andrew Marvell
items.stem: Which celebrated 1650 political poem by Andrew Marvell contains the famous lines describing the execution of Charles I: 'He nothing common did or mean / Upon that memorable scene, / But with his keener eye / The axe's edge did try'?
items.explanation: 'An Horatian Ode' captures the tragic majesty of Charles I's execution at Whitehall while acknowledging Cromwell as an irresistible force of providential destiny.

items.title: Quiz Q#354 · Andrew Marvell
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Andrew Marvell
items.stem: In which philosophical retirement poem by Andrew Marvell does the speaker praise solitude among trees, withdrawing the mind into contemplation: 'Annihilating all that's made / To a green thought in a green shade'?
items.explanation: 'The Garden' (1681) is Andrew Marvell's metaphysical ode on solitude, nature, and the Edenic retreat of the contemplative intellect.

items.title: Quiz Q#355 · Andrew Marvell
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Andrew Marvell
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"To a green thought in a green shade"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Andrew Marvell's The Garden (1681).

items.title: Quiz Q#356 · Andrew Marvell
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Andrew Marvell
items.stem: Which nine-stanza poem by Andrew Marvell in rhyming octosyllabic couplets contrasts the restless vanity of political ambition and sexual passion with the transcendent ecstasies of solitude in nature?
items.explanation: 'The Garden' celebrates the pure pleasures of plant life and contemplative solitude, presenting a spiritual retreat superior to earthly courts and wars.

items.title: Quiz Q#357 · Andrew Marvell
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Andrew Marvell
items.stem: In which iconic carpe diem poem does Andrew Marvell's speaker plead with his lover to seize the day, famously observing: 'The grave's a fine and private place, / But none, I think, do there embrace'?
items.explanation: 'To His Coy Mistress' (1681) is Marvell's celebrated carpe diem lyric, urging passionate haste before 'Time's winged chariot' and the dust of the tomb overtake beauty.

items.title: Quiz Q#358 · Andrew Marvell
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Andrew Marvell
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Had we but world enough, and time"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Andrew Marvell's To His Coy Mistress (1681).

items.title: Quiz Q#359 · Andrew Marvell
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Andrew Marvell
items.stem: Which Metaphysical masterpiece by Andrew Marvell is structured as a strict three-part classical syllogism: 'Had we but world enough, and time...' (thesis), 'But at my back I always hear...' (antithesis), and 'Now therefore...' (synthesis)?
items.explanation: 'To His Coy Mistress' deploys a brilliant syllogistic argument in rhymed tetrameter couplets, transforming a conventional love plea into a profound meditation on mortality.

items.title: Quiz Q#360 · Anne Bradstreet
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Anne Bradstreet
items.stem: Which 1650 volume of poetry, published in London by John Woodbridge without the author's knowledge, is celebrated as the first published book of poetry by an English author residing in the American colonies?
items.explanation: The Tenth Muse Lately Sprung Up in America (1650) by Puritan poet Anne Bradstreet was the first published literary work by a North American colonial poet.

items.title: Quiz Q#361 · Anne Bradstreet
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Anne Bradstreet
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"I am obnoxious to each carping tongue"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Anne Bradstreet's The Tenth Muse (1650).

items.title: Quiz Q#362 · Anne Bradstreet
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Anne Bradstreet
items.stem: Which early American poetry volume opens with a spirited Prologue in which the female poet defiantly counters misogynistic critics: 'I am obnoxious to each carping tongue / Who says my hand a needle better fits'?
items.explanation: Anne Bradstreet's The Tenth Muse (1650) challenged contemporary gender prejudices while establishing an authentic poetic voice in Massachusetts Bay.

items.title: Quiz Q#363 · Miguel de Cervantes
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Miguel de Cervantes
items.stem: In Miguel de Cervantes' masterpiece Don Quixote, which country hidalgo Alonso Quixano loses his wits from reading chivalric romances and sets out across Spain with Sancho Panza as a knight-errant?
items.explanation: Don Quixote de la Mancha is the titular knight-errant of Cervantes' novel (1605/1615), whose delusions transform windmills into giants and innkeepers into castellans.

items.title: Quiz Q#364 · Miguel de Cervantes
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Miguel de Cervantes
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"The brave man carves out his fortune."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Miguel de Cervantes's Don Quixote (1605).

items.title: Quiz Q#365 · Miguel de Cervantes
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Miguel de Cervantes
items.stem: Which monumental novel by Miguel de Cervantes, published in two parts in 1605 and 1615 and translated into English by Thomas Shelton, founded the modern European novel through its metafictional parody of romance?
items.explanation: Don Quixote revolutionized world literature by contrasting romantic idealism with earthy realism, translated into English by Shelton in 1612.

items.title: Quiz Q#366 · John Milton
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Milton
items.stem: Which companion poem by John Milton invokes the goddess Euphrosyne (Mirth) to celebrate the cheerful joys of rural daybreak, harvest festivals, and 'sweetest Shakespeare, Fancy's child'?
items.explanation: 'L'Allegro' (1645) celebrates the pastoral and social pleasures of daytime, paired with the nocturnal contemplation of 'Il Penseroso'.

items.title: Quiz Q#367 · John Milton
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Milton
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Hence, loathed Melancholy."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in John Milton's L’Allegro (1645).

items.title: Quiz Q#368 · John Milton
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Milton
items.stem: Which lyric poem in octosyllabic couplets by John Milton, published in his 1645 Poems, banishes 'loathed Melancholy' to depict an idealized day of active, lighthearted rustic and civic pleasure?
items.explanation: 'L'Allegro' portrays the joyful speaker's engagement with pastoral work, village folklore, and London comedy, opening with the banishment of melancholy.

items.title: Quiz Q#369 · John Milton
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Milton
items.stem: In John Milton's 1671 four-book epic Paradise Regained, which central figure overcomes Satan's temptations of appetite, imperial power, and Greek philosophical wisdom in the desert?
items.explanation: Jesus Christ is the divine protagonist of Milton's Paradise Regained (1671), whose spiritual obedience in the wilderness undoes the Fall of Adam.

items.title: Quiz Q#370 · John Milton
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Milton
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Abash'd the devil stood."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in John Milton's Paradise Regained (1671).

items.title: Quiz Q#371 · John Milton
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Milton
items.stem: Which brief epic in four books was published together with Samson Agonistes in 1671, written after Milton's Quaker friend Thomas Ellwood asked: 'Thou hast said much here of Paradise lost, but what hast thou to say of Paradise found?'
items.explanation: Paradise Regained (1671) is Milton's concise biblical epic dramatizing Christ's spiritual victory over Satan's wilderness temptations, fulfilling Ellwood's challenge.

items.title: Quiz Q#372 · John Milton
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Milton
items.stem: In which 1644 prose tract addressed to the Parliament of England does John Milton deliver his classic defense of freedom of the press, declaring that 'a good book is the precious life-blood of a master spirit'?
items.explanation: Areopagitica (1644) was Milton's passionate denunciation of the Licensing Order of 1643, championing open intellectual debate and free expression.

items.title: Quiz Q#373 · John Milton
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Milton
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"A good book is the precious life-blood."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in John Milton's Areopagitica (1644).

items.title: Quiz Q#374 · John Milton
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Milton
items.stem: Which 1644 classical oration by John Milton takes its title from the Athenian hill where the ancient court met, arguing against prior censorship and licensing of printed books?
items.explanation: Areopagitica (1644), modeled on an oration by Isocrates to the Athenian court of the Areopagus, argued that truth will always prevail in an open encounter.

items.title: Quiz Q#375 · John Milton
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Milton
items.stem: Which companion poem by John Milton invokes 'divinest Melancholy' to celebrate solitary study at midnight, philosophical musing in a lonely tower, and the solemn organ music of a cloistered cathedral?
items.explanation: 'Il Penseroso' (1645) praises the contemplative, intellectual life of quiet retirement, paired with the joyful extroversion of 'L'Allegro'.

items.title: Quiz Q#376 · John Milton
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Milton
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Hence, vain deluding Joys."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in John Milton's Il Penseroso (1645).

items.title: Quiz Q#377 · John Milton
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Milton
items.stem: Which poem by John Milton, published in 1645, opens with the banishment 'Hence, vain deluding Joys' and prays to walk unseen with the 'pensive Nun, devout and pure' through shadowy groves?
items.explanation: 'Il Penseroso' depicts the scholarly life devoted to Plato, tragedy, and hermit contemplation, matching the octosyllabic meter of 'L'Allegro'.

items.title: Quiz Q#378 · John Milton
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Milton
items.stem: In John Milton's Paradise Lost, which majestic rebel archangel awakens his fallen legions on the fiery lake of Hell and resolves 'to do aught good never will be our task, / But ever to do ill our sole delight'?
items.explanation: Satan is the commanding, tragic antagonist of Paradise Lost (1667), whose defiance in Books I and II led William Blake to declare Milton 'of the Devil's party without knowing it'.

items.title: Quiz Q#379 · John Milton
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Milton
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"To justify the ways of God to men."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in John Milton's Paradise Lost (1667).

items.title: Quiz Q#380 · John Milton
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Milton
items.stem: Which landmark twelve-book epic poem in English heroic blank verse was written by John Milton in total blindness to 'assert Eternal Providence, / And justify the ways of God to men'?
items.explanation: Paradise Lost (1667 in 10 books, 1674 in 12 books) is the greatest epic poem in the English language, recounting the war in Heaven and the Fall of Man.

items.title: Quiz Q#381 · John Milton
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Milton
items.stem: In John Milton's pastoral elegy Lycidas, which mourner ('the uncouth swain') weeps for his Cambridge classmate Edward King, invoking the Muses and 'Sisters of the sacred well'?
items.explanation: The uncouth swain is the pastoral shepherd-poet in Lycidas (1638), mourning the drowned youth and questioning the fleeting nature of poetic fame.

items.title: Quiz Q#382 · John Milton
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Milton
items.stem: Which 1638 pastoral elegy by John Milton mourns the drowning of Edward King in the Irish Sea, featuring St. Peter's fierce warning to corrupt clergy and the enigmatic image of the 'two-handed engine'?
items.explanation: Lycidas (1638) is Milton's pastoral elegy combining personal grief, classical myth, and prophetic denunciation of the Laudian clergy.

items.title: Quiz Q#383 · John Milton
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Milton
items.stem: In John Milton's 1671 closet tragedy Samson Agonistes, which blind Danite hero, captive at Gaza and mocked by the Philistines, pulls down the pillars of the temple upon his tormentors?
items.explanation: Samson is the tragic protagonist of Samson Agonistes (1671), who moves from despair and humiliation to spiritual regeneration and heroic self-sacrifice.

items.title: Quiz Q#384 · John Milton
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Milton
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Eyeless in Gaza at the mill with slaves."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in John Milton's Samson Agonistes (1671).

items.title: Quiz Q#385 · John Milton
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · John Milton
items.stem: Which 1671 drama by John Milton, modeled strictly on classical Greek tragedies with a Chorus of Danites and observation of the dramatic unities, concludes with the phrase 'calm of mind, all passion spent'?
items.explanation: Samson Agonistes (1671) adhered to Aristotle's Poetics and the models of Sophocles and Euripides, embodying Milton's definition of true tragic catharsis.

items.title: Quiz Q#386 · Richard Crashaw
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Richard Crashaw
items.stem: Which 1646 poetry collection by Metaphysical poet Richard Crashaw displays ecstatic Counter-Reformation Baroque intensity in devotional poems dedicated to Saint Teresa of Avila, including 'The Flaming Heart'?
items.explanation: Steps to the Temple: Sacred Poems, with other Delights of the Muses (1646) established Crashaw's reputation for lush, mystical Baroque Catholic verse.

items.title: Quiz Q#387 · Richard Crashaw
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Richard Crashaw
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Hail, sister springs."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Richard Crashaw's Steps to the Temple (1646).

items.title: Quiz Q#388 · Richard Crashaw
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Richard Crashaw
items.stem: Which 1646 volume of sacred verse took its title as an explicit homage to George Herbert's The Temple, but diverged into Catholic Baroque imagery of weeping wounds, bleeding hearts, and mystical ecstasy?
items.explanation: Crashaw's Steps to the Temple (1646) paid homage to Herbert in its title while embracing the sensory devotional fervor of the Continental Counter-Reformation.

items.title: Quiz Q#389 · Henry Vaughan
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Henry Vaughan
items.stem: In which landmark 1650 Metaphysical devotional collection by the Welsh poet-physician Henry Vaughan does the visionary poem 'The World' open with 'I saw Eternity the other night, / Like a great ring of pure and endless light'?
items.explanation: Silex Scintillans (1650/1655) is Henry Vaughan's devotional masterpiece, celebrating mystical encounters with nature, childhood innocence, and divine light.

items.title: Quiz Q#390 · Henry Vaughan
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Henry Vaughan
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"I saw Eternity the other night."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Henry Vaughan's Silex Scintillans (1650).

items.title: Quiz Q#391 · Henry Vaughan
items.meta: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era · Henry Vaughan
items.stem: Which collection of Metaphysical religious verse, subtitled 'Sacred Poems and Private Ejaculations' in tribute to George Herbert, bears a Latin title meaning 'The Flashing Flint' and features a heart struck by lightning on its title page?
items.explanation: Silex Scintillans (1650) signifies the hard, flinty human heart struck by the fire of divine grace to produce tears and sparks of holy devotion.
